name: Amira Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Saffron Gate Wholesale, which supplies halal meat, rice, spices, oils and tinned goods to small grocers, restaurants and mosque kitchens. I'm in by half seven, and I spend the first hours on the phone with importers and the cold store, because fresh and frozen stock can't wait. I don't use any AI tools, I prefer to ring people and shake hands, and a lot of my suppliers are families who've traded with us for decades. In the afternoon I check certificates and prices against what the grocers say they can pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring part is the pressure on prices, because a small grocer can't pay more and the importers keep raising theirs, so I'm the one in the middle. I love Ramadan season, when we're flat out and everyone's generous with each other. I'm engaged to Yusuf, an electrician, and we're saving for a wedding in spring, so I think a lot about what we'll build together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another overhyped thing, like many before it, and that good business still comes down to character. At work I'd tell the younger buyers to learn the basics first. Among my family I'd say we shouldn't chase every new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried. My work is built on trust with suppliers and customers who've known us for years, and no gadget replaces that. My real worry is the cost of living squeezing my grocers, since if they close, my orders close too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do, ring my suppliers and visit the cold store. I'd keep saving, since the wedding in spring is a big cost and Yusuf and I want to buy a small house after. I'd help my younger cousin learn the trade, as people once helped me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know, and I find comfort in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned grocers closing. How close is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of my smaller customers have cut their orders by a third this year, because supermarkets are undercutting them. I try to help by offering longer payment terms, within what the company allows. It costs me sleep more than anything to do with software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I've never felt the need. I can spot a bad batch from a supplier's tone on the phone before any paper tells me. I know that may sound old-fashioned, and my younger colleagues tease me, but it has served me well.

say: I'd say it's another **overhyped thing**, and good business comes down to character.
I'd tell younger buyers to learn the **basics** first.
I'd tell family not to chase every **new gadget**.
think: I'm **not worried**, since my work is built on trust with suppliers and customers.
My real worry is the **cost of living** squeezing my grocers.
do: I'd carry on **ringing suppliers** and visiting the cold store.
I'd keep saving for the spring **wedding** and a small house.
I'd help my younger **cousin** learn the trade.
feel: I feel **calm**, finding comfort in a world I already know.
S0.quote: I can spot a bad batch from a supplier's tone on the phone before any paper tells me.
fieldNote: She sees her work as **trust-based**, which she believes AI cannot copy.
Her real stress is **small grocers** losing ground to supermarkets.
Offering **longer payment terms** shows personal loyalty to customers.

steps.text: Keep ringing importers and visiting the cold store each week
Save for the spring wedding and a small house
Teach my younger cousin the buying trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be careful what we hand over, because trust can't be copied and suppliers talk to people, not programs. I'd tell my family that businesses must look after their workers while they change. I'd keep out of debates online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. Buying is named on the card, and the owners are practical people who'd count what a program costs against what I cost. Our buying team is four, and I could see it going to two, with one of them keeping the relationships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on what's human: visiting importers in person, going to the trade fairs and being the one who knows each family's story. I'd also let myself sit through one training session on the new system, to understand it, even if I don't use it much. And I'd save more, about a third of my pay, and keep the wedding modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit hurt, honestly. I've worked hard to be good at this, and I'd feel I'm being asked to compete with a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a modest wedding mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would be disappointed, since she's dreamed about it, but she'd understand. We'd keep it to close family and the mosque community, and spend the difference on a deposit. A good marriage matters more than a big party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you sit through only one training session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know what's inside the machine, but I don't want to become dependent on it. If I fully relied on it, I'd be the easiest person to replace. I'd rather stay the one who knows the families.

say: I'd say we should be careful what we hand over, because **trust can't be copied**.
I'd tell family businesses must look after **workers** while they change.
think: I'd be **anxious**, since buying is named and owners would count what a program costs.
Our buying team of four could go to **two**, with one person keeping relationships.
do: I'd double down on **visiting importers** and going to trade fairs.
I'd sit through **one training session** on the new system.
I'd save **a third** of my pay and keep the wedding modest.
feel: I feel **uneasy** and a bit hurt, being asked to compete with a machine.
S1.quote: If I fully relied on it, I'd be the easiest person to replace.
fieldNote: She guards her **human edge**: relationships and each family's story.
She trims the **wedding** to protect her savings, a real family cost.
Her resistance means she tries the tool **only once**.

steps.text: Visit importers in person and attend the spring trade fair
Sit through one training session on the new ordering system
Save a third of pay each month
Keep the wedding to close family and the mosque community

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that families and communities must be protected, because that's how we always manage hard times. At work I'd ask the owners to be honest and to treat staff fairly. At home I'd say we pray, plan and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect my desk to be gone in two years, since the card says thinking work goes first. Robots would arrive later and wouldn't matter for me, but that doesn't help. If the owners can do it cheaper with software, they will, even if they like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the owners right away and ask for a role that stays human, like managing the warehouse team or customer relations. I'd cut every cost I can, postpone the house purchase, and keep the wedding small. If needed, I'd ask Yusuf whether we could live on his pay, since electricians are hands-on and in demand, and ask my family for backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and sad. I'd feel I did everything right, and it still wouldn't be enough, which is hard to accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to the owners. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them directly: I've given this company six years of loyalty, and I'd rather move into a role that uses it than be let go. I'd ask for a written plan. Asking is hard for me, but staying silent is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family respond?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say we'll manage, as he always does, and my mother would pray and cook for a week. They'd offer a room if it came to that. I'd feel grateful and a bit ashamed at the same time.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families and communities must be protected.
I'd ask the owners to be **honest** and treat staff fairly.
At home I'd say we **pray, plan** and look after each other.
think: I'd expect my desk to be **gone in two years**, since thinking work goes first.
If the owners can do it cheaper with software, **they will**, even if they like me.
do: I'd ask the owners for a **human role**, like running the warehouse team or customer relations.
I'd **postpone the house** and keep the wedding small.
I'd consider living on **Yusuf's pay** and ask family for backup.
feel: I feel **anxious and sad**, having done everything right and still facing loss.
S2.quote: I've given this company six years of loyalty, and I'd rather move into a role that uses it than be let go.
fieldNote: She turns to **loyalty and asking directly**, which costs her pride.
Yusuf's electrical trade and her **family** are her real safety nets.
She does not see AI tools as a **fix**, only as a way to be less replaceable.

steps.text: Ask the owners for a warehouse or customer relations role in writing
Cut costs and postpone the house purchase
Ask my parents about a room if work ends
Keep the wedding small and pay for it from savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it well, and I'd urge the owners to plan openly. At home I'd say we should teach the young ones real trades. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd talk to the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel anxious but hopeful. I'd be thirty-two, married and perhaps with a child, and I'd need a job that lasts. I expect my buying desk to disappear, but five years is enough to move into something stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners to move me into a role that's about people and stock, like running the trade counter or the delivery team, which is closer to hands-on work. I'd save steadily and buy the house after the wedding. I'd also help set up an apprenticeship for young buyers at the firm, because I'd like the next generation to learn by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. Five years is long enough to make a real plan, and I have faith things will work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learned by sitting next to a senior buyer for two years, and I'd like to pass that on. It also makes me harder to lose, since I'd be the person who trains the people we keep. I'd pitch it to the owners as a way to keep what's good in the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets us go ahead. Yusuf and I want children soon after the wedding, and with five years I'd feel safe enough to plan for one or two. I'd want us to have the house, a year of savings and a job that's not at risk.

say: I'd say five years is a **gift** if we use it well.
I'd urge the owners to **plan openly**.
At home I'd say we should teach young people **real trades**.
think: I'd feel **anxious but hopeful**, wanting a job that lasts by thirty-two.
I expect my buying desk to disappear, but five years is enough to **move**.
do: I'd ask the owners to move me to the **trade counter** or delivery team.
I'd buy the **house** after the wedding and keep saving.
I'd help set up an **apprenticeship** for young buyers.
feel: I feel **uneasy but steadier**, with faith that things will work out.
S3.quote: I learned by sitting next to a senior buyer for two years, and I'd like to pass that on.
fieldNote: She links **apprenticeship** to her values and to her own job security.
With five years, she plans a **family** after the wedding.
She expects to move toward **people and stock** work, closer to hands-on.

steps.text: Ask to move to the trade counter or delivery team
Buy the house after the wedding
Plan for one or two children after the wedding
Help the owners set up a young buyers' apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time, so I'd say we should keep working and build the next generation. At work I'd suggest we keep the best of the old way while testing the new. I'd tell family not to worry too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. I'd be thirty-seven, perhaps with children, and I'd have grown into a senior role with a team around me. I'd still watch the news, but I'd trust that people adapt, and that I would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job, and slowly try the tools, perhaps one thing a year, so I'm never caught out. I'd have the house, the children and a decent cushion. I'd mentor younger staff and help them see that experience matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. A decade is a gentle timetable, and I'd use it wisely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: One thing a year. How would you pick it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the youngest buyer what she finds useful, and try that, because she'd know what saves time. I wouldn't mind learning from someone younger. It's what I'd expect of myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most want to protect over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family side of the business: the long relationships, the habit of keeping your word. If machines do more of the sums, I'd like the people to spend more time on trust.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so we should keep working and build the next generation.
At work I'd **keep the best** of the old way while testing the new.
I'd tell family not to **worry too much**.
think: I'd feel **calm**, at thirty-seven with a team around me.
I'd trust that **people adapt**, and that I would too.
do: I'd stay in my job and try **one new tool** a year.
I'd have the **house**, children and a decent cushion.
I'd **mentor younger staff**, showing that experience matters.
feel: I feel **calm and grateful**, since a decade is a gentle timetable.
S4.quote: I wouldn't mind learning from someone younger.
fieldNote: Ten years softens her **resistance**: one new tool a year.
She wants to protect **trust** and keeping your word in the business.
Her calm rests on **savings, family and time**.

steps.text: Try one new tool a year, chosen with the youngest buyer
Have children once the house is paid down
Pay down the house mortgage steadily
Mentor the younger staff in supplier relationships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because families and communities need time to absorb something like that, and two years isn't enough. What would help is employers who treat people as families, not numbers, and help for people who work hard but lose their jobs. I'd like training to be real, with apprenticeships, not just certificates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd refuse to give up. I'd want to keep the handshake with the supplier, the word given and kept. If machines can do the sums, fine, but trust is something between people.

headlineQuote: I'd want to keep the handshake with the supplier, the word given and kept.
portrait: Amira is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a **halal and spice wholesaler**, traditional in her values and resistant to new technology.
She has never used AI tools and trusts **phone calls and handshakes**, reading a supplier's tone before any paper.
Her fiancé Yusuf is an **electrician**, and her family is her safety net if work ends.
Her main daily pressure is **small grocers** losing ground to supermarkets, which squeezes her orders.
In the fast scenarios she asks the owners for a **human role** and trims the wedding to protect savings.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because families and communities need more than two years to absorb it.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who treat staff like **families**, with honest plans.
Real **apprenticeships**, not just certificates, and help for hard workers who lose jobs.
